title: Ang 508–517: Gujri ki Var M3
tomorrow: what would it look like to love with your eyes, ears and tongue?

lines: A GATE SMALLER THAN A SEED.
cards: Some arguments get stuck in a strange place: you're right, you know you're right, and every time you say so, the way back to the other person gets narrower.
On ang 509, inside the third Guru's ballad, Kabir describes exactly that jam. A gate smaller than a mustard seed. A mind swollen up like an elephant.
How does it get through? And right after his question, the Guru answers.

teach.h: A BALLAD BY THE THIRD GURU.
teach.b: Gujri ki Var is Guru Amar Das's ballad: pauris, his own stanzas, each with saloks set before it.
Near its start sits a salok by Kabir. In paraphrase: the gate of liberation is narrow, a tenth of a mustard seed.
The mind has swollen into an elephant. How can it pass through? It's a funny picture, and a sharp one.
The gate isn't shut. Nobody's guarding it. The problem is the size of what's trying to get in.
Sikh teachers hear the elephant as haumai, the ego, the self that keeps getting bigger every time it insists. Then the very next salok is Guru Amar Das's, and it answers.

teach.h: THE GURU'S ANSWER: IT OPENS WIDE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: if one meets such a True Guru, who is pleased and shows grace, the gate of liberation opens wide, and one comes and goes with ease.
So the Granth sets a Bhagat's question and a Guru's answer on the same page, a conversation across the lines. And notice the answer doesn't tell the elephant to try harder. Pushing only jams it.
The gate opens when the self stops filling the doorway and grace has room to work.
That's the third's ballad: a gate too small to force, and a Guru who says it was never meant to be forced.

how: Ragis sing the Granth's vars salok by salok and pauri by pauri; in Gujri ki Var of Guru Amar Das, Kabir's salok of the narrow gate is followed by the Guru's reply.

o: where Guru Amar Das's ballad in Gujri begins
where Guru Arjan's ballad in Gujri begins
a page of Kabir's sayings about elephants

games.q: the narrow gate — tap the pairs.
p: with grace, the gate opens wide

s: Kabir and Guru Amar Das both speak in Gujri ki Var
Kabir asks how the elephant mind will fit; Guru Amar Das answers in the next salok.
the narrow gate means only a few special people get through
it's narrow for the swollen mind; the Guru's answer is that it opens wide.
the answer is to push harder until the elephant fits
pushing only jams it; the gate opens when the self stops filling the doorway.

games.q: you and your brother both want the car on saturday. you have the better reason, and you've said so several times now. by the narrow gate, what's the next move?
o: stop arguing the reason and ask him what he needs it for.
say it once more, calmly; being right is being right.
give him the car and stay quietly annoyed about it.
games.why: Kabir's elephant isn't wrong, just too big for the gate. the Guru's answer is the self making room, not the argument getting louder.

practice: Let your shoulders drop, lower your chin a little, and rest your hands small in your lap: the elephant folding itself down. Stay in that smaller shape for the sit, breathing easily, nothing to push.
If you'd like, read the two saloks on ang 509 first.
